title: Sort employees by name alphabetically (case-insensitive).

s1_definition.profdef: Case-insensitive alphabetical sort uses `Comparator.comparing(Employee::getName, String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER)`, which orders by the name key using a comparator that ignores letter case. This prevents all-uppercase names from sorting separately from lowercase ones.
s1_definition.analogy: The front-desk officer at the National Bank of India wants the customer list in alphabetical order for a phone book, but some names were typed in capitals and some in small letters. A plain sort would wrongly put all the capitals before all the small letters. A case-insensitive sort treats "amit" and "Amit" the same, so the list reads naturally A to Z.
s1_definition.oneliner: Sort names with `String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER` so capitals and lowercase are ordered together, not separately.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Case-insensitive alphabetical sort uses `Comparator.comparing(Employee::getName, String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER)`, which orders by the name key using a comparator that ignores letter case. This prevents all-uppercase names from sorting separately from lowercase ones.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The front-desk officer at the National Bank of India wants the customer list in alphabetical order for a phone book, but some names were typed in capitals and some in small letters. A plain sort would wrongly put all the capitals before all the small letters. A case-insensitive sort treats "amit" and "Amit" the same, so the list reads naturally A to Z.

**One line to remember:** Sort names with `String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER` so capitals and lowercase are ordered together, not separately.

sections.s2_technical:
A naive sort on strings uses their natural ordering, which compares by the underlying character codes. In that encoding all uppercase letters come before all lowercase letters, so "Zebra" would sort before "apple" — clearly wrong for a human-readable alphabetical list. The fix is a case-insensitive comparator.

The `Comparator.comparing` factory has a two-argument form that takes both a key extractor and a comparator for the key. Passing `Employee::getName` as the key extractor and the built-in constant `String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER` as the key comparator gives a comparator that sorts by name while ignoring case. So "amit", "Amit", and "AMIT" all sort to the same position.

An equivalent approach extracts a normalised key, for example `Comparator.comparing(e -> e.getName().toLowerCase())`, which lower-cases before comparing. The CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER constant is cleaner because it does not allocate a new lowercase string per comparison, but the lower-casing approach is sometimes used when you also want to strip accents or apply other normalisation.

A senior nuance: case-insensitive is still not fully locale-correct for all languages, because alphabetical order and case folding vary by language. For truly locale-aware ordering — sorting names in a specific language's conventions — you use a `Collator` configured for that locale. For English names the case-insensitive comparator is the right, simple answer.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India is printing an alphabetical staff phone book, but the HR data has names in inconsistent casing — some all capitals, some normal, some lowercase from a bad import. A plain sort would group all the capitalised names ahead of the lowercase ones, which looks wrong. This is exactly how a case-insensitive sort works — names are compared ignoring case, so the directory reads naturally from A to Z.

The code defines an `Employee` with a name. A `PhoneBookService` exposes `byNameCaseInsensitive(List<Employee>)` using the case-insensitive comparator. The runnable `Main` feeds mixed-case names and logs the alphabetical order.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: four mixed-case names — rajesh (lowercase), Priya, AMIT (uppercase), neha.

Step 1: The stream opens and sorted buffers all four names because it is stateful.

Step 2: The comparator extracts each name and compares using the case-insensitive order, which folds case so AMIT is treated as if it were amit, Priya as priya, and so on.

Step 3: Compared case-insensitively the order is amit, neha, priya, rajesh, which maps back to the original-cased names AMIT, neha, Priya, rajesh.

Step 4: Had we used a plain natural-order sort instead, AMIT and Priya, being capitalised, would wrongly have come before neha and rajesh because uppercase letters have smaller character codes — the case-insensitive comparator avoids exactly that.

Step 5: The source list is unchanged; a new ordered stream was produced.

Step 6: `collect` gathers the alphabetical order into a new list.


sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: [rajesh, Priya, AMIT, neha]   (mixed case)
    │
    ▼
  stream()  (stateful buffer)
    │
    ▼
  sorted(comparing(getName, CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER))
    fold case → compare: amit < neha < priya < rajesh
    │
    ▼
  [AMIT, neha, Priya, rajesh]   (natural A–Z, case ignored)
    │
    ▼
  collect(toList())  →  new ordered list
    (plain sort would wrongly give: AMIT, Priya, neha, rajesh)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
To sort names alphabetically while ignoring case I use the two-argument form of Comparator.comparing, passing the name getter as the key extractor and the built-in constant for case-insensitive order as the key comparator. That gives a comparator which orders by name but folds case, so an all-uppercase name and a lowercase name sort to the same place and the list reads naturally from A to Z.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India this was for an alphabetical staff phone book. The HR data had names in inconsistent casing — some all capitals, some normal, some lowercase from a bad import — and a plain sort would have grouped all the capitalised names ahead of the lowercase ones, because in the underlying character encoding uppercase letters come before lowercase, which would put a name like Zebra before apple. The case-insensitive comparator fixes exactly that.

A senior point I always raise is that case-insensitive is still not fully locale-correct for every language, because alphabetical order and case folding differ across languages. For truly locale-aware sorting — ordering names according to a particular language's conventions — I would use a Collator configured for that locale rather than the simple case-insensitive comparator. For English names, though, the case-insensitive order constant is the right and simple answer, and like every sort it leaves the source list untouched and produces a new ordered stream.
